displayQuote: They didn't have any rights to the land and there was no reason for anyone to grant them rights which they had not conceived and were not using

meta.title: Who really said "They didn't have any rights to the land and there was no reason for anyone to grant them rights which they had not conceived and were not using"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: Ayn Rand said it about Native Americans in a Q&A at West Point on March 6, 1974. It is not from The Virtue of Selfishness.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They didn't have any rights to the land and there was no reason for anyone to grant them rights which they had not conceived and were not using'?
meta.ogDescription: Ayn Rand said it in the Q&A after her West Point lecture of March 6, 1974. Here is the transcript from the recording, and how the quote gets misplaced.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Rand said this about Native Americans in the question-and-answer session after her lecture “Philosophy: Who Needs It” at the U.S. Military Academy, West Point, on March 6, 1974. The wording is confirmed in a transcript taken from the official recording. She said it out loud; it does not come from any of her books or essays.

source.heading: The West Point Q&A, March 6, 1974

source.excerpt: And, since the Indians did not have any property rights—they didn’t have the concept of property; they didn’t even have a settled, society, they were predominantly nomadic tribes; they were a primitive tribal culture, if you want to call it that—if so, they didn’t have any rights to the land, and there was no reason for anyone to grant them rights which they had not conceived and were not using. It would be wrong to attack any country which does respect—or try, for that matter, to respect—individual rights, because if they do, you are an aggressor and you are morally wrong to attack them.
trail: Salon’s Ben Norton bought the official MP3 of the West Point lecture and Q&A from the Ayn Rand Institute’s online store, and says the quotes in his piece are taken directly from it. The full line appears word for word in his Salon transcript (Oct. 14, 2015) ↗.
Wikiquote’s sourced Ayn Rand page ↗ lists the line in its 1970s section and credits it to the Q&A after her address to the West Point graduating class on March 6, 1974.
On Talk:Ayn Rand ↗, editors listened to the recording. One confirmed “she did say those things,” and a 2018 timestamped transcription has the same sentence at about 19:20 into the Q&A.
The Ayn Rand Institute’s Ayn Rand Lexicon ↗ confirms the March 1974 lecture to West Point’s graduating class and lists separate lecture and Q&A recordings.

source.rightsNote: These are spoken remarks from 1974. They survive in a recording that the Ayn Rand Institute sells, and an edited version appears in the later collection Ayn Rand Answers. That is well after the 1931 cutoff, so treat the wording as in copyright. Quoting a single sentence for commentary is a different question from who owns the rights.

author.name: Ayn Rand
author.heading: About Ayn Rand
author.bio: Ayn Rand was born in Russia and emigrated to the United States. She wrote The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged and founded the philosophy she called Objectivism. In her later years she lectured widely, including a March 1974 address to West Point’s graduating class, and the question-and-answer sessions after her talks were often recorded.

misattribution.heading: Where the quote goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Rand did say it, so the attribution holds. What usually goes wrong is the source, and the way the sentence gets joined to other lines.

items.why: A Wikiquote contributor noted that other websites credit this quote to Rand’s essay collection The Virtue of Selfishness. She said it aloud at West Point, so it is not in that book (Talk:Ayn Rand ↗).

items.who: “[The Native Americans] didn’t have any rights to the land…”
items.why: The long version that circulates adds a bracketed subject and uses ellipses to join sentences she said at different points in her answer. A Wikiquote editor removed it for a while for those reasons, and later editors described it as paraphrase with sections left out (Talk:Ayn Rand ↗).

The printed text in this collection reads “rights that they had not conceived of,” and says “Any European” where the recording has “white person” (Talk:Ayn Rand ↗). Salon says this transcript “is full of errors” and puts her remarks in a different order (Salon ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The popular wording matches what Rand said in the West Point Q&A on March 6, 1974, as transcribed from the official recording (Salon ↗).

context.heading: Why this line keeps resurfacing
lead: Rand came to West Point in March 1974 to lecture the graduating class on why philosophy matters. A cadet then asked how she could hold such a positive view of America given the treatment of Native Americans, the enslavement of Black Americans and the internment of Japanese Americans. She answered at length, arguing that people who had no concept of property rights could not claim rights to the land.

The lecture was later published, but the Q&A stayed obscure. Salon reports that the Ayn Rand Institute offered the recordings free online until about October 2013 and then moved them to its paid store. Salon published the full transcript in 2015, and the line has been a standard exhibit in criticism of Rand ever since.
detailsBody: The sound quality of the recording is reported to be poor. Independent transcriptions differ in small ways, such as “continent” or “country” in a later sentence. The sentence on this page reads the same in Salon’s transcript and in the Wikiquote talk-page transcription.
The links to the Ayn Rand Institute audio files quoted on the Wikiquote talk page no longer work. The official recording is sold through the Institute’s store.
